World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: The 'internationally acclaimed' French sculptor who is nowhere to be found
World.content:
An Australian gallery said their artist was an "internationally acclaimed" Parisian sculptor. Then the story changed.

Eliza Murley is standing outside a Melbourne art gallery, peering through a large glass window.

She's there with the ABC to see a particular piece of art. But on the street — where the wind is whipping up a frenzy — is as close as she can get.

Ms Murley — a former gallery worker — is not comfortable going inside. The ABC has been banned from entering.

The artwork in question is a wall sculpture — dark green, about a metre long, and selling for just under $7,500. It looks like a giant, crumpled sticky note — one of many produced over the years by an artist called Jean Paul Mangin.

"He's Parisian," Ms Murley says, recounting the spiel workers would give buyers when selling his art.

" He is internationally acclaimed for his work … he's practising out of Paris, and his artworks are shipped to us from Paris. "

For years, this supposedly famous Frenchman has been selling sculptures through Ms Murley's former employer — an Australian gallery called Studio Gallery Group.

But there's a problem: no-one has been able to find him; no-one has been able to verify that this character exists.

"Clients would want more info, and I just couldn't provide it," Ms Murley says.

Mr Mangin has no website, no social media and no LinkedIn.

The ABC has been unable to contact him in Australia, and there's no trace of him in France.

It's not until 2021 — when Studio Gallery group first introduces Mr Mangin to the Australian market — that his name, his story, and his art start to appear.

Studio Gallery Group is selling Mangin's La Grazon for almost $7,500. ( )

The sculptures are made from colourful sheets of plastic that have been bent and moulded. They come in different shades, finishes and sizes and are listed for sale between $2,000 and $10,000 each.

For years, each piece comes with the same 100-word artist bio:

"Internationally acclaimed and collected French sculpturist, Jean Paul Mangin's work largely draws from his own intimate and emotional experiences of life.

Loading Instagram content

"The artist feels the translation and physical embodiment of his oeuvre not only defines his future but creates a dialogue with the outside world, ultimately providing a safe place to heal, flow, and articulate.

"Jean Paul speaks through his mediums such as recyclable plastics and polymer materials. The plasticity and very fluid nature of his materials offer a poignant metaphor of our shifting individual experiences within our changing world, how we see ourselves in relation to/in conversation with our surrounding environments."

The social media accounts of Studio Gallery Group and gallerist Ms Armstrong echo these claims about Mr Mangin: his global reputation, his Parisian studio.

"A much awaited shipment from Paris! Seductive, sculptural works from Jean Paul Mangin have now arrived (worth the wait!)…" one Instagram post reads.

Mr Mangin quickly becomes a bestseller for the gallery, his art featured in glossy magazines and coveted by trendy designers.

But over the years, questions have circled the gallery: who is Jean Paul Mangin?

Why would a commercial gallery — a family-run business — go to such extreme lengths to protect his identity?

Why would they threaten to take the public broadcaster to court to block these questions from being answered?

The artist

When Studio Gallery Group launched in 2016, it was a passion project for painter and gallerist Kerry Armstrong.

Studio Gallery Group is, by all accounts, commercially successful. Ms Armstrong worked with her husband, Michael Armstrong, and her daughter, Lauren Elyse, to grow one commercial Melbourne gallery into five exhibition spaces across three states. It now sells the works of more than 100 artists.

Ms Armstrong has stated publicly that her business model is for artists to make money.

"We have had an identity crisis around that," Ms Armstrong told the Not Super. Woman podcast in 2025.

"I believe what we've done with Studio Gallery's definitely changed it."

Five years in, the gallery took on Jean Paul Mangin.

From the moment his works started to arrive, Mr Mangin stood out to staff.

"Michael [Armstrong] would come into the gallery with them [the sculptures], half wrapped in bubble wrap … and just put them on the ground," former Melbourne gallery worker Molly told the ABC.

"Molly" — a pseudonym the worker is using in order to speak publicly — said Mr Mangin's works had none of the hallmarks of an international art delivery.

Interview with Molly ABC: What does proper packaging look like? Molly: If it’s a rolled-up artwork, then in a tube with bubble wrap and protective sleeves… and then if it’s a sculpture in a wooden nailed box with padding on the inside. ABC: And same game for international shipments? Molly: Yeah. ABC: And how did these ones come? Molly: Just bubble wrap. ABC: Is that standard practice? Molly: No.

There was no box, no shipping label, no consignment notice, and no tax declaration form.

Just bubble wrap.

"Sometimes not even sticky tape," said another former Sydney gallery worker, Kelly M, who is withholding her last name to protect her identity in the industry.

"It was quite ad hoc and not what you'd expect for an $8,000 sculpture from Paris."

The second thing that stood out to Ms M was the speed in which some pieces were being shipped.

If buyers wanted something different to what was on the gallery walls or in the back catalogue, they could commission the artist to make a custom piece.

Typically, those orders took months. But former gallery staff said Mr Mangin's commissions often arrived within weeks.

"Things were arriving very fast," Ms M said.

Studio Gallery Group has five locations across Australia. ( )

Studio Gallery Group started selling Mr Mangin's works in 2021. ( )

The ABC spoke to 11 former Studio Gallery Group employees who worked across the gallery's five locations over a period of four years, managing art, artists, buyers and transport.

Collectively, they painted a picture of Mr Mangin as a man who was uncontactable, and who appeared to be absent from decisions concerning the display and sale of his artwork.

"They would arrive without any hanging mechanism," said Ms Murley, the former Melbourne gallery worker.

The sculptures also showed up without instructions on how they should be hung; there was no indication which way was up or down.

"Myself and Michael would often just take a look at the works and decide where we wanted to put a hook or a hole in the piece so that we could hang it on the wall," Ms Murley said.

"And then Michael would just drill it in there."

Several former workers said they found it surprising that the gallery was making so many choices on Mr Mangin's behalf.

" Maybe this Jean Paul person doesn't care," said ex-worker Abby, who is also using a pseudonym."But I've never met an artist that didn't care. "

Abby dealt with artists and buyers at the gallery. When she tried to contact Mr Mangin directly via an email address on file, she said she never got any response.

It didn't matter if the question related to commissions, sales, or the title of his artworks. When it came to Mr Mangin, Abby and other gallery workers told the ABC that they were always directed to go through Ms Armstrong or her daughter, Ms Elyse. The reasons varied.

"Kerry's explanation was that he's had some sort of trauma and doesn't speak to anyone from the outside world," Abby said.

Other workers said they were told Mr Mangin was a "recluse" and only liked to talk to Ms Armstrong; that there was a language barrier only she could overcome; that questions should be directed to Mr Mangin's assistant.

None of the workers ever dealt directly with this nameless assistant, but they were referenced whenever new Jean Paul Mangin sculptures needed a title.

The naming convention was, and still is, a French word connected to the colour of the piece, followed by a number.

Names like "Papier" for white sculptures, "Cassonade" for dark brown, "Metal Mou" for gold, and "La Grazon" for dark green.

But some of those titles don't pass elementary French. "Le gazon" means grass in French, but "grazon" is not a word; it's an American brand of weed killer.

Mr Mangin's French credentials, similarly, don't stack up.

ABC searched for the artist Jean Paul Mangin in Paris. ( )

No artist by the name of Jean Paul Mangin is registered to pay taxes in France. ( )

There was no record of Jean Paul Mangin at La Maison Des Artistes. ( )

The ABC travelled to Paris to see whether Mr Mangin, as a French artist, was listed on the national art registry — La Maison Des Artistes.

He wasn't.

There was also no artist called Jean Paul Mangin registered to pay tax in France.

And so, another question emerged: if there's no French artist by the name of Jean Paul Mangin, who is making his art?

The art

A long way from Paris, in Sydney's west, another artist pulls on a pair of gloves to retrieve a bright blue piece of plastic from a giant industrial oven.

Amid the hum of factory machines, she sets to work quickly transforming the flat sheet into a sculpture.

It's a race against time — two minutes until the plastic goes hard.

Her hands glide over the material, pressing it up and down to create hills, caverns and folds. She looks like she's dancing.

Ms Pesce uses the plastic PMMA to create her sculptures. ( )

Ms Pesce has just two minutes to sculpt her piece. ( )

In two minutes, she's finished her sculpture. It looks strikingly similar to Mr Mangin's; a giant, crumpled sticky note.

The woman is Anya Pesce, an Australian artist who's spent over a decade refining her practice. She's exhibited all over the world, including in France.

Like Mr Mangin, Ms Pesce uses the plastic PMMA — polymethyl methacrylate — to create her pieces.

Like Mr Mangin, she was represented by Studio Gallery group for three years. He joined the gallery because she left.

"She [Ms Armstrong] explained to me that she'd always wanted to show him, but since I was with the gallery, she couldn't," Ms Pesce told the ABC.

Loading...

Before Ms Pesce was able to retrieve all her artwork from the gallery, Mr Mangin's sculptures were already hanging on the walls and on Studio Gallery Group's social media.

Online, people were confused about whose work was whose.

"Other artists were still tagging my name to works that were appearing that were his," Ms Pesce said.

In a bid to find out more about this mysterious artist, Ms Pesce enlisted a friend to email Ms Armstrong, posing as a prospective buyer asking for information.

In her response, Ms Armstrong wrote that Mr Mangin had applied to work with the gallery in 2019 but was rejected.

"We saw a material similarity to one of our artists who was represented at that time by our Victorian galleries," Ms Armstrong said in her email.

"So as much as we were extremely excited by the work and could see differences, out of professional loyalty, we couldn't consider his work, even for a different state."

The email also name-dropped Mr Mangin's manager — someone named Anthony Seymour — and filled in some details about the artist's past.

"Jean Paul personally shuns contact," Ms Armstrong wrote.

"He I am told has trauma regarding an accident as a younger man and whilst we have met Anthony, for now the work will speak for Jean Paul."

But Ms Pesce still had questions. She decided on a different approach.

Anya Pesce has accused Studio Gallery Group and Mangin of copying her work. ( )

In late 2021, Ms Pesce enlisted a lawyer who wrote to Ms Armstrong, alleging, among other things, that Mr Mangin and Studio Gallery Group had copied her work — same materials, colours, and techniques.

Ms Pesce is not the only artist who makes sculptures out of flat, coloured plastic, and just because two things look similar does not mean copyright infringement has occurred.

Ms Pesce, via her lawyer, also requested information: Mr Mangin's contact details, his qualifications and professional background, proof of his works being made and shipped from Paris to Australia, and the terms of his contract with Studio Gallery Group (a contract that several former workers told the ABC they could not find in the system).

In response, Ms Armstrong's lawyer did not answer any of the questions and alleged Ms Pesce had made a series of empty claims. The letter demanded an apology and said, without one, Ms Armstrong could take legal action of her own.

That marked the end of things between Ms Pesce and Ms Armstrong until 2025, when Ms Pesce was approached by Australian Associated Press (AAP) journalist Liz Hobday for a story. The AAP article aired Ms Pesce's theory that Mr Mangin's art was a rip-off of her own sculptures, and that she didn't believe he was an internationally acclaimed French artist working out of Paris.

Hear the full story Listen: Inside the search for the mysterious French artist. A three-part podcast by Background Briefing.

Studio Gallery Group refused to answer any of Ms Hobday's questions pre-publication, but she heard from them post.

"After the story was published, AAP received several legal letters from their lawyers," Ms Hobday said in a statement.

"AAP stands by its reporting and the original story is still available to read on our website."

Ms Pesce also received a legal letter, as did an arts website that published their own version of the AAP story.

The arts website took the piece down and published an apology. Ms Pesce said she went back to square one.

"I dig every day, I know others dig every day and there are still no answers," she said.

"If there's any truth to this… show us."

The Gallery

A year later, in January 2026, the ABC too had its first unexpected dealing with Ms Armstrong's legal representation, in the foyer of a grand five-star Sydney hotel.

It was days after a man named Simon Dulhunty reached out to the public broadcaster with a text message.

Hi Julia. It's Simon calling regarding the Studio Gallery. I understand you have been asking around and I've got a lot of knowledge about the facts and would like to catch up for a coffee or tea in the next couple of days. I'm in Sydney.

Hi Simon, great to hear from you. That sounds fabulous. I can work around you. How does tomorrow suit?

According to his LinkedIn at the time, Mr Dulhunty was a journalist and media executive who was now working as a media advisor for no specified employer.

He met the ABC in the lobby cafe of Sydney's Fullerton Hotel, dressed in a crisp, blue business shirt and suit pants.

It quickly became clear that Mr Dulhunty was not a source. He was there as the media manager of the law firm Giles George, on behalf of its clients: Jean Paul Mangin, and Studio Gallery Group's directors, Kerry and Michael Armstrong.

His message to the ABC was clear: back off the story and stop asking questions about Mr Mangin. If not, the public broadcaster could expect a "very heavy-handed legal response".

The ABC has since received 12 legal letters from Giles George, including one vowing to take the public broadcaster to court to block the story.

In the Fullerton Hotel lobby, during that Thursday morning coffee, Mr Dulhunty too made a case for the gallery. He placed a clear plastic sleeve full of paper documents on the table that he claimed proved Mr Mangin was a real person, and suffering incredible distress because of this investigation.

He pointed to the top of the stack — the front page of a confidential report about Mr Mangin.

On it, in bold, was written "Jean Paul Mangin (nom de plume)"

That was the first time the ABC learned that Jean Paul Mangin was not the artist's real name.

And that raised another question: Why has this never been mentioned before?

Studio Gallery Group later said, in a statement to the ABC:

"Jean Paul Mangin is the nom de plume of a real artist — a long-established and protected artistic practice."

Mr Dulhunty said that Studio Gallery Group and Ms Armstrong had always been transparent about the nom de plume.

But there's no mention of this detail in any of the gallery's online marketing materials.

Former workers told the ABC that this detail was news to them.

"I wonder why they felt the need to keep that from their staff," Ms Murley said.

But it's not just Mr Mangin's name that's fabricated.

During that meeting, Mr Dulhunty told the ABC that the artist's backstory was also "an elaboration".

Mr Mangin is not French (but has "French heritage"). He is not based in France. His works are not being shipped from Paris.

He is also not necessarily a "he".

In response to ABC questions about the gallery's online representations of Mangin, Studio Gallery Group said:

"Studio Gallery is responsible for marketing of the artists they represent…

"Studio Gallery has audited its current marketing material relating to Jean Paul Mangin and have no concerns. Jean Paul Mangin continues to be an extremely popular artist whose works are and will continue to be cherished by collectors.

"We respect the right of this artist and in fact all creators to use nom du plumes [sic]."

But Molly and other former workers were concerned the gallery had lied to buyers.

"My god … that's how they were selling him and marketing him," Molly said.

Ms Hobday, the AAP journalist, and Ms Pesce, the artist, told the ABC that they were not aware Jean Paul Mangin was a nom de plume.

Rebekah Gay, an advertising lawyer at Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer, would not draw any conclusions about Mangin and Studio Gallery Group, but said any money-making business was required under Australian Consumer Law to be honest about the quality and origin of any products its selling.

The ABC cross-referenced the gallery's plastic orders with subsequent social media posts of Jean Paul Mangin artworks.

The same rules apply to commercial galleries.

"Saying that a product comes from country A versus country B is very likely to be problematic," Ms Gay said.

While there is nothing wrong about an artist using a fake name, Ms Gay says their backstory needs to be accurate.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission — the national watchdog — declined to comment on the case.

Among its online claims, Studio Gallery Group said that Mangin's work was being shipped from Paris. But the ABC has confirmed that the gallery itself ordered more than a dozen sheets of plastic from a local Melbourne supplier in 2021.

The orders were colourful: mirrored sheets in gold, bronze, grey, orange, blue and green; matte finishes with names like "Mineral Grey", "Desert Beige", "Candy Blue", "Moonlight", and "Lime Zest".

The ABC cross-referenced these orders with subsequent social media posts of Jean Paul Mangin artworks. The broadcaster found the colours and finishes appeared to match.

The Name

Although there is little online about Mangin, there is ample content about Studio Gallery Group and its gallerist, Ms Armstrong.

Through several tell-all interviews and troves of social media posts, she has documented her life — her leap of faith to working as an artist; her recovery from brain surgery; her childhood living in the country surrounded by horses; her husband and kids.

Armstrong has documented her work, life, and family online.

It's online — underneath one of Ms Armstrong's Facebook photos — that the ABC found a final clue about Jean Paul Mangin.

The comment is from a user named John Mangan. His account is locked, but lists where he lives and where he grew up. That information leads the ABC to an obituary and a cemetery in country Victoria.

Benalla is a few hours' drive north-east of Melbourne; Ned Kelly country.

Off the Hume highway and over the train tracks is a big, flat, grassy field covered in a grid system of gravestones. A cemetery.

Each plaque is topped with a bouquet of fake flowers.

A Facebook comment led the ABC to a gravesite in regional Victoria. ( )

Each plaque at Benalla cemetary is topped with fake flowers. ( )

In Row S, Plot 64, lies a headstone framed by two upturned horseshoes. It reads:

"John Paul Chalwell Mangan… 1.4.1922 — 27.7.2011."

The late 89-year-old is buried with his wife. Engraved at the bottom of the plaque are the names of their five children.

John Mangan — the man who commented on Ms Armstrong's Facebook post — is one of them.

The other four are Michael, Joanne, Anthony, and Kerry Armstrong.

John Paul Mangan is Ms Armstrong's late father; his name just a few letters different from the nom de plume of the internationally acclaimed Parisian artist she exhibits in her gallery: Jean Paul Mangin.

Which means, whoever Jean Paul Mangin truly is, they're someone Ms Armstrong views with enough favour and sympathy to let them meet the world disguised in her own father's name.

John Paul Mangan is buried beside his wife, Pamela Anne. ( )

Studio Gallery Group did not respond to questions from the ABC about the identity of Jean Paul Mangin, or how similar that name is to Ms Armstrong's late father. Kerry and Michael Armstrong also did not respond to questions and refused the ABC's multiple invitations for an interview.

Ms Armstrong's daughter Lauren Elyse did not respond to questions. Neither did Jean Paul Mangin, who the ABC attempted to contact via Studio Gallery Group.

Instead, Studio Gallery Group issued three separate statements via their lawyer. In the first one, they said:

"Studio Gallery Group categorically rejects the premise, tone and methods of Background Briefing's investigation, which reflects a sustained and harmful campaign against one of its artists.

Jean Paul Mangin is the nom de plume of a real artist — a long-established and protected artistic practice. Despite being put on notice of serious psychological harm to this artist, efforts to unmask this individual have continued, raising grave concerns about privacy, safety and ethical responsibility…

…There is no legitimate public interest in exposing the identity of an artist whose work is lawfully created and sold, and whose anonymity is protected for legitimate reasons."

In a second statement, they also said:

"Studio Gallery is responsible for marketing of the artists they represent…

... Studio Gallery has audited its current marketing material relating to Jean Paul Mangin and have no concerns..."

The third statement, sent shortly before the release of this episode, is attributed to Michael Armstrong.

It said that Jean Paul Mangin had been represented by the gallery under a nom de plume since 2021, having participated in this genre for many years prior.

Michael Armstrong also said:

"The circumstances around the creation and adoption of their pseudonym are strictly confidential and we will not betray the trust this individual has placed in us...

... While we are disappointed by the misinformation peddled by a few disenfranchised individuals, Jean Paul Mangin continues to be one of our most in demand artists — the mystery surrounding their identity fuelling interest in their stunning work.

The artist has not listened to this series or engaged with the ABC prior to broadcast. They have been solely focused on their artistic practice."

Credits

Reporting: Julia Bergin

Illustrations: Teresa Tan

Digital production: Justine Landis-Hanley

Photography: Darryl Torpy, Jack Fisher, Nathan Laine, Annie Brown

World.title: Family history drives Wallaroos star in Anzac Day Test against NZ
World.content:
Any time Piper Duck pulls on a Wallaroos jersey is a special moment.

Piper Duck's grandfather Keith served with the RAAF during World War II. (Supplied: Duck family)

But playing in the historic Anzac Day Test against New Zealand holds even greater significance for the Wallaroos back-rower.

Three generations of Duck's family served in Australia's military forces.

Her beloved grandfather Keith, who died in 2013, was a leading aircraftman with the RAAF during World War II.

Duck only recently discovered her great-grandfather, Ernest, also served in World War II.

And during the peacekeeping efforts in East Timor, her uncle Glenn was a member of the Royal Australian Regiment.

The sacrifices they made are not lost on Duck.

Piper Duck's uncle Glenn was part of Australia's peacekeeping efforts in East Timor.

While she does not compare sport to military service, the 25-year-old feels honoured to be given a chance to represent Australia on such an important day for the nation.

"It means a lot to me," Duck said.

"I don't think we can ever repay the service they gave to this country, and the genuine significance of what that means and what they've done for Australia and this community."

Leonard to become Wallaroos' most-capped player Rugby was not on Michaela Leonard's radar when she was a child in Canberra, but she is about to achieve a historic milestone when the Wallaroos meet the Black Ferns on Anzac Day.

In the lead-up to Saturday night's Test at Sunshine Coast Stadium in Kawana Waters, Duck and her Wallaroos teammates have become more familiar with Australia and New Zealand's shared military history.

"We've been learning about the Anzacs more thoroughly in camp," she said.

"We've learned what they went through, and the morals and values they held around mateship, and the genuine camaraderie that they shared in those times.

"We can never repay the service they gave, so to represent them in any way is really important to me and I want to do them proud in doing that."

ABC Sport will live blog the Wallaroos vs Black Ferns Test from 7pm.

Duck believes a similar sense of solidarity exists in rugby, especially among the Wallaroos squad.

"I love the game of rugby; the contact, the physicality it brings," she said.

"But I also love the camaraderie, the mateship, the genuine love we have for each other and the culture we build in rugby.

"I think it's pretty incredible in the female game."

'Monumental' moment

The Wallaroos and Black Ferns have been playing each other since 1994, but this weekend's Test will be the first held on Anzac Day.

Australasian rugby has never genuinely settled on a marquee match on April 25 in the way the AFL (Collingwood vs Essendon) and NRL (St George Illawarra vs Sydney Roosters) have in their men's competitions.

The Wallaroos-Black Ferns Test is an opportunity for rugby to establish a regular fixture on Anzac Day and pay respect to those who served both nations.

Piper Duck feels the Anzac Day Test can have a profound impact on Australian women's rugby. (Getty Images: Stu Forster)

It will also help elevate women's rugby in Australia with a standalone event.

Duck, who has been named on the Wallaroos' reserves bench, wants the Anzac Day Test to have an annual presence on the sporting calendar.

After tornado warnings and midnight matches, Wallaroos are ready for NZ Having survived the threat of tornadoes during their US tour, the Wallaroos are enjoying a distraction-free build-up to their Anzac Day Test against New Zealand.

"I would love it," she said.

"I think it has every possibility to be able to do that. I think it shows how far female sport has come to get a Test match like this against the Black Ferns.

"It's monumental for the female game. I'm really excited to see the numbers who turn out.

"What it means for both Australia and New Zealand — I think this could become a really big moment for sport in general, to get two national sides on Anzac Day who do have such a strong, rich history competing in the game.

"I think it would be spectacular to keep going long-term."

How Duck came to rugby

Growing up in the Riverina town of Tumut, Duck was largely unaware that rugby existed.

The sport did not come into her orbit until she was 15, when the Australian women's rugby sevens team won gold at the 2016 Olympics in Rio de Janeiro.

Piper Duck was inspired by Australia's rugby sevens win at the Rio Olympics. (Getty Images/World Rugby: Dan Mullan)

"I always loved contact sport but it just wasn't offered," said Duck, who will play her 26th Test on Saturday night.

"So I actually started refereeing rugby league very young. I was the first female rugby league ref in the Riverina — I think when I was 13, 14 — because rugby for women just wasn't really known, especially in rural regions.

"In 2016, when Sharni Williams and the sevens girls played at the Olympics, I was sitting on the couch and turned on the TV … I thought women weren't allowed to play.

"I had never even seen rugby union before and here it is, this game, and I'm like, 'Oh my God, since when was this a possibility?'.

"I was pretty amazed. That was a massive movement in rugby union at the time as a lot of young girls have come off the back of that and gone, 'Wow, this is a possibility for me.'"

Piper Duck will play her 26th Test for the Wallaroos on Saturday night. (Getty Images/ CameraSport)

Duck's love for rugby grew even further when she left Tumut to attend Sydney's Barker College, where she helped start a girls team at the school.

She hopes the Wallaroos' Test against the Black Ferns can inspire greater female participation in rugby, in the same way she was drawn to the sport after Australia's Olympic success 10 years ago.

"We often say, 'You can't be what you can't see', and that was the moment for me," Duck said.

The Wallaroos and Black Ferns will be competing for the O'Reilly Cup across two Tests this season.

They will meet again in Auckland on August 22.

Saturday's match is the final stop in the Pacific Four Series, which also features Canada and the USA.

World.title: James Valentine knew good radio and I was his wide-eyed apprentice
World.content:
About ten years ago the phone rang in the triple j office in Melbourne and a voice on the other end said: "Do you wanna come on the radio with me?"

I had just started working at the ABC after years at community radio station Triple R and now ABC Radio Sydney talkback star and professional saxophonist James Valentine was suggesting we do a music segment together.

Before becoming a broadcaster James Valentine (centre) played sax with rock band The Models in the 1980s. (Supplied: Countdown Magazine)

There was, even in that first call, a magic to the way James conducted the world around him — full of risk, play and his delight in both.

James didn't check that I could string a sentence together. He just seemed to trust that he would bring out whatever he needed to in me, this music person. And so began one of the great tutelages of my life. The kind you can only dream of.

What began as a 15-minute weekly chat about music evolved into years together doing a segment on basically anything but. When I finally got the chance to walk in his loafers as an ABC Radio Melbourne host we devised inter-state segments that joined our shows together.

About ten years ago the phone rang and a voice on the other end said simply, "Do you wanna come on the radio with me?“

The power of a mentor

This is not the article I planned to write.

A month or so ago, I had a long and wonderful conversation with James. The plan was that an article would be published before he died. It was my job to celebrate his influence while he was alive and could read what I wanted to say.

Perhaps I was fooling both of us. I wasn't ready to accept his dying and we both knew that was why I was writing it. These were to be his last months.

I reminded him in that recent phone call — the last time we spoke — of a moment some years back when I asked him on air if he would attend my funeral.

"Well, yes, if we're still on the radio together," he answered. "But unlikely if we're not."

I laughed. It was so true. We both knew he meant more to me than I could ever mean to him.

James had a world of family and friends, he told me during that call, that put me at about 220 on his list of people who mattered to him. I delighted in this. There is no greater show of love than an accurate reflection of your place in someone's life, and I was chuffed to make it into the top 200 (well, a smidge over).

I told him how mortifying it was that although we had not made radio together for a while, I was the dork who wanted to be at his.

If you're lucky, you get to learn from the best doing something you love. The role of the mentor is difficult to equate to any other relationship — it's part admiration, part study, part trying to show you are worthy of it. If you are lucky, this relationship might be one of the most transformative of all.

James Valentine pictured during a live broadcast with Jacinta Parsons. (Supplied: Jacinta parsons)

I collected moments like a hoarder

Throughout our years working together I was covertly studying everything he did.

I considered myself his apprentice. Perhaps non-consensual, perhaps not to his knowledge, but nevertheless I spent those years keenly listening to every strange and wonderful interaction he had with his audience.

I collected those moments like a hoarder, hoping that one day I would have the chance to use them doing what I had wanted to do since I was eight, when I recorded myself interviewing imaginary guests like Bob Hawke. I asked the questions and then gave the answers (as Bob), threw to a song, came back and welcomed the opposition leader.

I followed that little girl's fascination with radio broadcasting and James became the piece of the puzzle I had been waiting to meet.

In that March telephone conversation, James and I spoke about our time on radio together and those years where that music segment turned into the kind of absurd play that he was famous for.

There was an afternoon where we dared each other to see who could stay silent the longest and not crack under the pressure of silence on live radio. We were terrifyingly aware that at any moment the emergency music tape might kick in because the radio had gone dead.

We pushed each other and messed up each other's hair, and I felt like the little dog to his big, so happy was I to be in his on-air company.

Throughout our years working together I was covertly studying everything James did on air. (ABC Radio Sydney: Declan Bowring)

A servant to good radio

James was the broadcaster I wanted to be, beginning with those first radio shows that I made in my bedroom when I was a little girl.

He taught me I needed to be brave and to take risks, that safe radio was rarely good radio.

In dying, James Valentine taught us how to live James helped us make sense of life and gave us permission to laugh at the absurdity of it all — and ourselves.

During those segments, I practised on him, knowing he would be a willing teammate. I knew that whatever I threw at him, he would push it further. Good radio is fearless radio and he taught me the elusive element of radio craft that can't be taught but is learnt by watching and through trial and error.

James was a servant to good radio. There is much we should mandate in broadcasting from the Valentine school of radio: risk, play, mistakes, curiosity, deep listening. It was the kind of broadcasting that was unique, but shouldn't be.

Shock jocks have dominated a perception of what talkback radio is: a dominant male host, exploiting his audience for political and cultural power.

Instead, James brought a love of his audience. Not the cheesy earnest love of a clumsy practitioner, but rather, he understood the parts of us that made us loveable.

And then — this was the mastery — he knew how to turn those parts of our lives into raucous entertainment. He loved us in our most ridiculous moments. Watching James taught me how, in the absurd minutia of our lives, we reveal ourselves to each other.

His style of radio was not an earnest endeavour though, as likely it has been for me. I turned what I learnt from him into a PhD on talkback radio and its capacity for positive impact on its family of listeners.

I wanted him to know that I loved him by trying to be a good student. His best.

I declared that I had matched him in some areas — building absurdity into every part of my work. But there were areas that remained elusive.

… And the audience

I took notes on the studious way James would think about his audience. James saw his listeners as genuine creative collaborators.

In his galaxy, the audience needed to deliver gold and nothing less. He expected each of them to meet and exceed his standard. Of course they did, time and time again.

From him, I learnt one of my most valuable lessons: a good broadcaster doesn't make radio to an audience, they make it with an audience. The audience is where everything of worth is made, and their involvement is the only way it transcends into something that has the capacity to transform the way we see the world.

James knew his audience intimately and he got great satisfaction plumbing them for their best.

Even when there was suspicion a talkback topic wasn't working, his response was: "Never show fear. In fact, never feel it. Work it. Work it until you know your audience believes in whatever you are asking them to do, and they will back you up. They always do."

This kind of radio takes us beyond the horror of news. James's programs were anathemas to taking things too seriously.

But there lay another great lesson: radio needs to reflect the dynamism of life. One moment we laugh together, the next we cry together — as we are now commemorating the great loss he is in our lives.

James had a long career with the ABC and his audience grew to love him. (ABC/ ABC Radio Sydney: Declan Bowring)

"errrrmmmm"

James knew he was good.

Just like all the conversations we had over those years together on radio, the last one was real and raw and hilarious. I was a bit taken aback by the life I could hear in that James Valentine voice.

He still had that very Valentine way of saying "um", his comic sequitur, if you've heard him, you know that it would go something like this: outrageous proposal, followed by an "errrrmmmm", followed by additions to the outrageous proposal.

James Valentine swapped microphones — and found a new audience who loved him James Valentine started his career on the stage, but it was his time on radio that came to define him.

That "errrmmmm" will live in my skin.

During our last phone call we talked straight with each other. I told James that it was an honour to witness how "Valentine" he was in his accepting his death.

I asked him if he was scared and if he could understand the real absurdity of this criminally early death, leaving a family he adored and an audience he should have had years left to entertain.

He switched momentarily. He told me that he had accepted it, that he knew he had no other choice but to embrace it but that he found it bloody weird. How could he not be here with us all?

I will forever be James Valentine's apprentice, stealing the gold of his life's work.

I write this to honour his impact on my work and career, on audiences and colleagues, on the way we delight in our absurdity. But mostly on the impact he had on that eight-year-old girl, who will forever try her hardest to be nearly as good as him.

World.title: Live: Australians come together to mark Anzac Day
World.content:
"Welcome to the Dawn Service at the Australian War Memorial in Canberra where the time is 5:30," MC Scott Bevan says.

Shortly prior, Flight Lieutenant James Evans opened the ceremony with a didgeridoo performance.

"We assemble here, at this special place of remembrance on this day, symbolically close to the time that the first Anzacs – young men from Australia and New Zealand – landed on a Türkiye beach during the First World War," Mr Bevan continues.

World.title: In Farrer, One Nation has a shot at shattering the thickest glass ceiling
World.content:
Pre-polling opens on Tuesday for the by-election in Farrer two weeks from today.

A blockbuster contest beckons. The Liberals and Nationals are at serious risk of emerging as the primary losers.

But Labor, which is not running, is also at risk. Even if some in the party are privately munching from the popcorn bucket of schadenfreude at news this week the Coalition parties will direct preferences to One Nation's David Farley ahead of the independent Michelle Milthorpe.

Farley and Milthorpe are running neck-and-neck, according to some of the internal party polling this column has been told about.

If the numbers are right — always an important caveat — and the preferences flow the way Liberals and Nationals are urging their followers, Milthorpe faces an uphill battle.

Independent candidate for Farrer, Michelle Milthorpe. (ABC News: Philippe Perez)

This gives Farley a shot at shattering one of the thickest of political glass ceilings of the past three decades.

For all the heat and wind that Pauline Hanson has produced over the years, she and her party have never clinched a lower house seat in the federal parliament under their own steam.

A big reason for that is because the Liberals have tended to preference Labor ahead of One Nation.

Hanson was elected in 1996 after being disendorsed by the Liberal Party for controversial remarks about Indigenous Australians. It happened so late in the campaign that her name appeared on the ballot as a Liberal. She subsequently lost her seat in 1998.

For 30 years One Nation have been locked out of the House of Representatives while a raft of independents and teals have found repeat success, winning lower house seats, particularly in the two most recent elections.

Which is why Farrer may become a watershed moment in Australian politics.

Could One Nation burst through the gate?

"Three things have destroyed One Nation until now: no discipline, no decent vetting system for candidates, and they could never get preferences from the Coalition," former Queensland premier Peter Beattie tells this column.

The decision this week by conservative parties to exchange preferences "is a whole new ball game", he says.

A decision that has received relatively little national attention.

If Farley gets over the line, it will be in no small measure because Angus Taylor and Matt Canavan have endorsed that outcome.

They would prefer One Nation winning Farrer over an independent.

They have decided, in effect, that a potential backlash from the political right against the Coalition parties is more of a threat than a backlash from moderate Liberals and Nationals.

Either way, once considered the "barbarians" of the political right, One Nation would no longer be hollering through the gate.

They would have burst through.

If Farley gets over the line, it will be in no small measure because Angus Taylor and Matt Canavan have endorsed that outcome. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

"If they win Farrer, they'll get momentum out of it," Beattie says.

As well as political resources and credibility in the electorate as a destination for disenchantment.

Though Farrer is a NSW seat with specific local issues that matter to voters living on the banks of the Murray River — from Albury to the South Australian border — a One Nation win would have national consequences.

Beattie thinks that could "devastate" what is left of the Liberal Party's moderate vote in other parts of the country.

Those same moderates would be furious that their party's preference cards helped One Nation win.

A shrewd Queenslander, Beattie is well-versed in this topic. He recalls that in the 1998 state election — when Hanson was still riding the first great wave of her popularity — he refused to accept One Nation preferences.

The result was that Labor lost six seats to One Nation. The Nationals lost five. But Labor also picked up Liberal seats and formed a minority government.

Despite the initial hype after winning 11 seats, One Nation quickly disintegrated. And it's been politically largely irrelevant until its unexpected renaissance after last year's federal election devastated the Coalition.

Beattie now worries that One Nation winning a lower house seat would lure voters on the centre-right who are angry about the Albanese government but frustrated at the weakness of the Liberals.

Perversely "this could be the first time there's a threat to the Albanese government," he says.

Loading

Have they peaked too soon?

This may not be as fanciful as it seems on first blush. Labor does indeed have a 94-seat majority, but that was built on an historically low primary vote of just under 35 per cent.

National polls suggest that has fallen since the election. And One Nation is no longer all that far behind.

Voters who are disenchanted — and there appears to be quite a few in that camp, if surveys asking whether the "country is on the right track" are any guide — may decide that Farrer offers a salient lesson.

Namely that One Nation can be a vehicle for their dissatisfaction, drawing people who previously voted Labor.

"If Albanese and the Labor government loses support, you could end up with a rabble on the right that does threaten the government, with One Nation, the Nationals and the Liberals," Beattie says.

Canavan out in the cold in Farrer This week the Treasurer went west, the government made a major announcement well ahead of the budget and the Nationals leader got a little frosty in Farrer.

Beattie notes the recent political row over One Nation's rehiring of a convicted rapist is a sign the party is still prone to misjudgement and ill-discipline that turns voters off.

New recruit Barnaby Joyce admitted to Sky News this week the episode "would have affected the polls".

Indeed Newspoll this week recorded a drop in the One Nation vote from 26 per cent to 24 per cent. Labor was steady at 31 per cent and the Coalition was on 21 per cent.

How that plays out in Farrer over the final two week will be intriguing. Have One Nation peaked too soon? Or is the recent dip just noise in the numbers?

"We are in extraordinary unchartered waters," says Beattie. "I've never seen anything like it. The primary of major parties is down, disenchantment is up, Taylor has been a dud and hasn't lifted the Liberal vote in any way I thought he would.

"So where do unhappy people go? They're going to One Nation."

Nudged in that direction by Liberal and Nationals how-to-vote cards.

Jacob Greber is political editor of ABC's 7.30 program.

World.title: Israel's killing of journalists in Lebanon highlights the impunity with which it acts
World.content:
It has often been described as a stalemate this week — this war that is now primarily centred on the Strait of Hormuz.

Not even the financial markets seemed to react much to the latest presidential decrees this week, that seem to bear little connection to unfolding events.

This was even though, slowly but surely, the military confrontations in the strait have been escalating, with both sides striking, or seizing, each other's assets.

And the "stalemate" description came even though Trump had declared a ceasefire was underway in Lebanon, yet the two sides continued to launch assaults on each other.

In this war the claims and counterclaims — and their frequent detachment from reality — have become a story in themselves, as we try to line up what we can see and hear, with the various declarations of where the truth and strategic advantage may lie.

As Financial Times columnist Edward Luce wrote last month, it is a "strange situation where we await a statement from Iran to check whether there's any truth to what the US president is saying".

This of course was not Luce claiming the Iranians were the ultimate font of all truth, just a reflection of the lack of credibility that has been proved to be attached to pronouncements from the Trump administration.

The US President says Israel's ceasefire in Lebanon will be extended, but the broader conflict with Iran shows no signs of being resolved. (Reuters: Evan Vucci)

An important time for journalism

In such times, the work of journalists becomes crucial to what we know of how events are unfolding, and how that might affect us all.

Journalists can be our eyes and ears in the middle of the conflict — to the extent that they are allowed on to the battlefield. But they are also the people who compile, corral and verify the riot of information to which we are now bombarded.

News that the regime in Iran was killing thousands of its own people in protests only came out as it was pieced together by the media.

Journalists — and the media — are far from perfect. But their ability to do their job remains a vital barometer of our confidence in how we understand the world in which we live.

Civilians get killed. Aid workers get killed. But you may never know this unless there are journalists who can tell their stories, who can corroborate and check the conflicting accounts.

Journalists are much more regularly challenged, reviled and abused in this age of social media platforms and presidential late night social media posts.

But in general, the world still watches how they are treated, and demands they be respected when they are doing their job.

If nothing else, they are often the identifiable human faces of the people whose stories they are telling.

There was relief when this week a Kuwaiti court acquitted US-Kuwait journalist Ahmed Shihab-Eldin on all the charges he was facing after nearly two months in detention.

Ahmed, who has contributed to The New York Times, PBS, and Al Jazeera English, appeared to have been charged with spreading false information, harming national security and misusing his mobile phone after he posted verified video showing a US F-15 fighter jet falling from the sky and crashing near Kuwait City.

The jet was one of three that were mistakenly shot down by Kuwaiti air defences.

Mourners carry the body of one of the Palestinian journalists killed in an Israeli airstrike in Khan Younis. (Reuters: Ramadan Abed)

Why does Israel keep killing journalists?

But a shocking aspect of recent conflicts has been the overwhelming number of journalists killed by Israel.

The Committee to Protect Journalists reported in February that Israel was responsible for two-thirds of all press killings in both 2025 and 2024, two consecutive record years for press deaths.

More journalists and media workers were killed in 2025 than in any other year since the CPJ began collecting data more than three decades ago.

Journalists, by the nature of their jobs covering war, are at additional risk, and some of their deaths could have been accidental.

But it's not as if there aren't any other major brutal conflicts that have been going on in the world in the past few years. Ukraine and Sudan are just two that come to mind.

Israel posts fake photo of journalist it killed in strike The IDF has admitted the image of a killed journalist in military uniform it posted on its official X account was faked.

Yet it is Israel, which is supposed to be the great bulwark of democracy in a barbaric Middle East, that absolutely dominates the record books for its murder of journalists.

According to the CPJ, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) have committed more targeted killings of journalists than any other government's military since 1992.

Israel often defends its actions by claiming the journalists are militants disguising themselves in press flak jackets. These are often unsubstantiated claims based on flimsy evidence.

It's not just journalists who have been killed in these circumstances, as illustrated by the case of Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom and her colleagues. And no matter their profession, there is rarely a proper investigation carried out into such killings.

No-one has been held accountable for any of the murders of journalists we have sometimes witnessed with our own eyes, sometimes because Israeli jets or drones come back to strike wounded journalists and aid workers, and ambulances.

The IDF will often slow walk its responses, complicate them, or claim journalists were the victims of mistaken identity or the fog of war.

The majority of journalists killed by Israel have been Palestinians. With the international media barred from entering Gaza, their eyes were our only view into the horrendous siege that took place there.

Loading...

Israeli strikes kill Amal Khalil

Journalists continue to be killed in Gaza, and now an increasing number are being killed by Israel in Lebanon.

This week Lebanese journalists Amal Khalil, a reporter for the newspaper Al-Akhbar, and freelance photojournalist Zeinab Faraj were travelling in a convoy when the car in front of them was hit in a drone attack, killing the two people inside it.

The women's car was then hit by a grenade fired by another drone, forcing them to seek shelter in a nearby house.

That house was then targeted by fire from an Israeli jet. Faraj was eventually rescued but Khalil died under the rubble, after efforts to rescue her were reportedly obstructed by the Israeli military, which according to Lebanese officials also fired on the Red Cross and an ambulance that had come to their assistance.

The Israeli military said it struck the vehicle after identifying what it called an "immediate threat" linked to Hezbollah, and said it had received reports two journalists were injured as a result of the strikes. It denied it had obstructed rescue efforts.

Loading...

In an interview last year, Khalil claimed that she had received direct death threats from the IDF when hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah in Lebanon escalated into full-scale war in September 2024.

"They literally said 'we will separate your head from your shoulders'," she told the interviewer.

Khalil said she had always been aware of the risks of her job but, until then, had not taken particular precautions.

"They may tell me 'why do you want to do to this?' and I would say 'I am as equal as these people'," she was quoted as saying in translation.

"I may be be targeted, but as long as there is a woman in Houla, what happens to her happens to me."

She claimed she received "a direct target on my phone from the Mossad, from the Israelis. They threatened to murder me".

"They literally said 'we will separate your head from your shoulders if you do not leave the south, and we advise you to leave the south'.

"They even included in their messages, and it was many messages sent to my private phone, they included several messages with personal information about me to make me feel 'we know you well'."

Amal Khalil was from the south of Lebanon and she wanted to report on what was happening there, on what she called the desecration of whole neighbourhoods. (Reuters: Aziz Taher)

Israel acting with apparent impunity

Khalil was from a Shia village in the south of Lebanon and she wanted to report on what was happening there, on what she called the desecration of whole neighbourhoods.

The Israeli military said the incident was under review and claimed the vehicles had crossed a "forward defence line" after leaving a Hezbollah-associated military structure, posing a threat to forces on the ground.

It added that it "does not target journalists" and takes steps to reduce harm to them while ensuring troop safety.

However, the Union of Journalists in Lebanon said that when medics attempted to rescue the women, Israeli forces prevented access to the site and used stun grenades.

A senior Lebanese army official said that it was only about four hours later that rescue teams were able to enter the area, escorted by Lebanese army forces and in coordination with UNIFIL, and recover Khalil's body from the rubble.

Lebanese reports further said a Red Cross ambulance transporting one of the wounded journalists to hospital in Tebnine came under Israeli fire and showed visible bullet marks.

Loading

The Lebanese health ministry said Israeli forces "prevented the completion of the humanitarian mission" by firing a sound grenade and live ammunition at rescue teams and ambulances attempting to reach the scene.

The CPJ's regional director, Sara Qudah, said in a statement that "the repeated strikes on the same location, the targeting of an area where journalists were sheltering, and the obstruction of medical and humanitarian access constitute a grave breach of international humanitarian law".

"CPJ holds Israeli forces responsible for the endangerment of Amal Khalil's life and the injuries Zeinab Faraj sustained after the targeted strike on their location."

This is not just a story about the killing of journalists, bad as that may be.

But it is about the apparent impunity with which Israel now acts, the exceptionalism which it asserts, and the fact that — like the US president who has empowered the Israeli government — there appear no normal guardrails on its actions.

That applies not just to how it treats journalists and ordinary people, but how it strides the world stage and attempts to influence global events.

There are many bad, rogue states at work in the world these days. But the world has continued to back some of them, even when their actions no longer tally with the values we supposedly hold.

Laura Tingle is the ABC's global affairs editor.

World.title: Virginia Giuffre's legacy and the year that followed the Epstein files release
World.content:
Warning: This story contains graphic and distressing content, including testimony of sexual assault.

A year on from the death of Virginia Giuffre, the world is still unpacking the consequences of the files she helped bring to light.

If you or anyone you know needs help: 1800 Respect National Helpline: 1800 737 732

Men's Referral Service: 1300 766 491

Lifeline (24-hour crisis line): 13 11 14

Full Stop Australia: 1800 385 578

Bravehearts: counselling and support for survivors of child sexual abuse: 1800 272 831

Her story sparked a re-examination of accountability for those sitting in some of the world's most powerful seats with ties to convicted sex offender Jeffery Epstein.

The fallout continues to be felt around the world. A prince stripped of his title. Veteran politicians have stepped down. A former prime minister faces criminal charges, and business executives are no longer in plum roles with multi-billion-dollar brands.

Three of the 27 names listed below have been arrested.

Virginia Giuffre, with a photo of herself as a teen, when she says she was abused. ( )

Giuffre, who took her own life a year ago, didn't live to witness the full impact of the truths she brought forward.

She had long alleged she was trafficked for sex to Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor and other prominent figures by Epstein when she was a teenager.

But the arrests, resignations and the unravelling of reputations came in the wake of her decision to speak.

Here's where the fallout stands, one year on.

Royalty

Arrested: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor Andrew Mountbatten Windsor was stripped of his title earlier this year. ( ) The Duke of York Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, a former prince, was stripped of his royal and military titles and evicted from his mansion by his older brother, King Charles III, late last year following renewed pressure over his friendship with Epstein. Emails released by the US Justice Department in January showed the British royal stayed in contact with Epstein long after the American's conviction for trafficking and sex with a minor. The documents allege Mr Mountbatten-Windsor forwarded sensitive UK information to Epstein, including trade documents about Vietnam, Singapore and other places he had visited as a British trade envoy. He was arrestedin Februaryon suspicion of misconduct in public office over the allegations but has not been charged. Years earlier, Giuffre claimed she was trafficked three times to have sex with the then-prince, twice as a teenager. He settled a US civil lawsuit in 2022 brought by Giuffre while not admitting liability. An email from Epstein released last year appears to confirm that Mr Mountbatten-Windsor was photographed with Giuffre despite his repeated denials. Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor and Virginia Giuffre, seen with Ghislaine Maxwell on the right. ( ) Ties cut: Sarah Ferguson Britain's Sarah Ferguson, Duchess of York, leaves Westminster Cathedral at the end of the Requiem Mass, on the day of the funeral of Britain's Katharine, Duchess of Kent, in London, Britain, September 16, 2025. REUTERS/Toby Melville ( ) Charity ambassador Sarah Ferguson, the ex-wife of former prince Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, lost her Freedom of the City of York title in March over her links to Epstein. In the latest cache of emails, Ms Ferguson calls Epstein a "legend" and tells him to "just marry me". The following day, her charity Sarah's Trust, which supported humanitarian projects, announced its closure. In September, multiple British charities severed ties with her, saying it would be inappropriate for her to continue as a patron.

Politics

Arrested: Peter Mandelson British ambassador to the United States Peter Mandelson in London on June 18, 2025. ( ) Britain's ambassador to the US Peter Mandelson was arrested in February over suspicion of misconduct in public office following the release of emails which alleged he had leaked discussions on possible UK asset sales and tax changes to Epstein during the financial crash. Bank transfer documents also suggest Epstein sent cash to Lord Mandelson and his partner. The British politician was released on bail the following morning after more than nine hours of questioning. UK Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer has ordered an urgent inquiry into Lord Mandelson, who remains under investigation. The veteran politician was fired as ambassador to the United States last year after an earlier batch of emails showed him calling Epstein "my best pal" and advising him on seeking early release from jail. Lord Mandelson apologised in January to Epstein's victims and for maintaining his friendship with the disgraced financier. Under investigation: Thorbjørn Jagland Thorbjoern Jagland has not been charged with any crimes, but investigations are ongoing. ( ) Diplomatic immunity Thorbjørn Jagland, a former prime minister of Norway, is under investigation on suspicion of aggravated corruption following his ties with Epstein. The Norwegian police unit Økokrim searched his home a day after the Council of Europe lifted his diplomatic immunity in Feburary following details he allegedly asked Epstein for help financing an apartment in Oslo. Mr Jagland also allegedly discussed a visit to Epstein's private island, while Epstein asked for an introduction to Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov. He has denied wrongdoing and says he never visited the island. Mr Jagland, who has not been charged, was the chair of the Nobel Committee and secretary-general of the Council of Europe during the period covered by the released documents. "Among other things, Økokrim will investigate whether gifts, travel and loans were received in connection with his position," investigators said in a statement. Resigned: Børge Brende Norway's former Foreign Minister Borge Brende ad multiple dinners with Epstein over a two year period. ( ) President and CEO of the World Economic Forum Børge Brende resigned as head of the World Economic Forum (WEF) in February after his name appeared in the millions of Epstein files. Documents revealed the former minister of foreign affairs of Norway had dinners with Epstein in 2018 and 2019. At the time of the revelations, the WEF said it would carry out an independent review of Mr Brende's interactions with Epstein. He insists he knew nothing of Epstein's criminal record. Resigned: Mona Juul Norway's former Ambassador Mona Juul was suspended on suspicion of gross corruption. ( ) Norway's ambassador to Jordan and Iraq Mona Juul resigned as Norway's ambassador to Jordan and Iraq in February after she was suspended on suspicion of gross corruption while working at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Norwegian media reports in January revealed the children of Ms Juul and her diplomat husband Terje Rød-Larsen were set to receive $US5 million ($6.9 million) each in a will Epstein signed two days before he died. Resigned: Terje Rød-Larsen Terje Rod-Larsen, a former Norwegian diplomat is under investigation. ( ) CEO of the International Peace Institute Terje Rød-Larsen resigned as CEO of the International Peace Institute after a 2019 report revealed the institute had received $US650,000 ($922,000) in donations from Epstein's foundations. A statement from the board said Epstein's crimes were "hideous" and Mr Rød-Larsen had apologised for his poor judgement. The Norwegian diplomat is under investigation alongside his wife, Mona Juul, for complicity in gross corruption. They have denied wrongdoing. Resigned: Alex Acosta Alex Acosta was a top federal prosecutor in Florida at the time of Epstein's first sex crime case in 2004. ( ) US labor secretary Alex Acosta resigned as an ex-Trump US labor secretary in 2019 following backlash from his handlings of Epstein's sex trafficking charges in 2004. "As I look forward, I do not think it is right and fair for this administration's labor department to have Mr Epstein as a focus rather than the incredible economy we have today," Mr Acosta said in 2019. A top federal prosecutor in Florida at the time, Mr Acosta handled Epstein's first case involving sex with girls, which resulted in a punishment that was publicly criticised as too lenient. Resigned: Jack Lang Jack Lang is under investigation over alleged aggravated tax fraud laundering. ( ) Head of the Arab World Institute Jack Lang, the former culture minister of France, resigned as head of a Paris cultural centre in February over alleged past financial links to Epstein. The 86-year-old and his daughter Caroline, a well-known French actor, are under investigation over alleged aggravated tax fraud laundering after the family allegedly set up an offshore company with Epstein in the British Virgin Islands. Resigned: Morgan McSweeney Morgan McSweeney stepped down following public outrage over his decision to appoint Peter Mandelson as ambassador to the US. ( ) UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer's chief of staff Morgan McSweeney resigned as chief of staff to British Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer in Feburary, taking "full responsibility" for advising him to appoint Peter Mandelson as Britain's ambassador to the US. "The decision to appoint Peter Mandelson was wrong. He has damaged our party, our country and trust in politics itself," Mr McSweeney said in a statement. Resigned: Joanna Rubinstein Joanna Rubinstein visited Epstein's island with her family after he was convicted of sex crimes. ( ) Chair of Sweden for UN High Commission for Refugees Molecular biologist Joanna Rubinstein resigned as Sweden's head of fundraising for the UN refugee agency in February after she was shown to have visited Epstein's island with her family after he was convicted of sex crimes. The former head of the World Childhood Foundation in the US — which works to end child sexual abuse and exploitation — said she was aware of Epstein's criminal case at the time but not the extent of the abuse. "I was aware of the verdict at the time of the visit. What has subsequently emerged about the extent of the abuse is appalling and something I strongly distance myself from," Ms Rubinstein told Swedish newspaper Expressen. Resigned: Miroslav Lajčák Slovakia's former Foreign Minister Miroslav Lajcak texted Epstein in 2018 talking about women under 30. ( ) National security adviser to Slovakia's prime minister Miroslav Lajčák resigned as Slovakia's national security adviser after he texted Epstein in 2018 talking about women under 30. In 2017, he also asked Epstein to help get a female producer's movie on the shortlist for the Oscars. At the time, he was the country's foreign minister. Resigned: George J Mitchell Giuffre alleged Epstein told her to have sex with George Mitchell. ( ) Chair of the Mitchell Institute In February, George Mitchell resigned as the chair of the Mitchell Institute, which he founded, after his name featured 300 times in the Epstein files. The former US senator and former chancellor of the Queen's University of Belfast was also removed from the grounds amid the fallout. Years earlier, Giuffre alleged Epstein told her to have sex with Mr Mitchell, according to court documents unsealed in 2019. Mr Mitchell denied the allegation and said he had "never met, spoken with or had any contact with Ms Giuffre".

Business

Resigned: Peter Attia Dr Peter Attia, who has millions of follows on social media, appeared more than 1,700 times in the Esptein files. ( ) CBS News contributor Peter Attia resigned as a CBS News contributor in February after the researcher's name appeared more than 1,700 times in the latest trove of Epstein files. There are extensive discussions between the two about medical matters but also some crude conversations. "P***y is, indeed, low carb. Still awaiting results on gluten content, though," Dr Attia wrote in one email to Epstein sent in February 2016. The celebrity doctor, who has millions of followers on social media, said that he met with Epstein seven or eight times at his New York City home between 2014 and 2019, but never witnessed illegal activity nor saw Epstein accompanied by anyone who appeared to be underage. Resigned: Bob Kerrey Bob Kerrey said he met with Epstein to support The New School, a university he was president of at the time. ( ) Board chair of energy company Monolith Bob Kerrey resigned from the board of directors of a Nebraska clean-energy startup in February after files released by the US Justice Department revealed he had met and emailed Epstein after the latter pleaded guilty to procuring a minor for prostitution in 2008. The former Nebraska governor and US senator said he met with Epstein to support The New School, a university he was president of at the time. Resigned: Thomas Pritzker Thomas Pritzker maintained contact with Epstein and Ghilliane Maxwell as late as 2019. ( ) Executive chairman of Hyatt Hotels Thomas Pritzker resigned as executive chairman of Hyatt Hotels in February but remains the director of The Pritzker Organization. In February, the Guardian reported the 75-year-old suggested five models who would be "serving girls" at a dinner party should be guests instead, writing in an email that "this would be far more fun". The billionaire acknowledged his "terrible judgement" in maintaining contact with Epstein and Ghilliane Maxwell, who was sentenced to 20 years in prison in 2022 for conspiring with Epstein to sexually abuse minors. Resigned: Sultan Ahmed bin Sulayem Sultan Ahmed bin Sulayem had a close relationship with Epstein that spanned over a decade. ( ) Chair and CEO of DP World Sultan Ahmed bin Sulayem resigned as chairperson and chief executive of DP World — a global logistics company — in February after documents revealed he had a relationship with Epstein that spanned more than a decade. In one email, Epstein called the Emirati business leader a "best and trusted friend". Resigned: Leon Black Leon Black remains under investigation by multiple regulatory bodies for his relationship with Epstein. ( ) CEO of Apollo Global Management Leon Black resigned in 2021 after documents revealed he paid Epstein more than $US150 million for "financial advice" over a five-year period. In March, US senator Ron Wyden wrote a letter to the Wall Street billionaire and said Mr Black was one of Epstein's primary sources of income, "flooding him with cash at a time when he was already a registered sex offender". Mr Black has denied wrongdoing but remains under investigation by the US Senate. Resigned: Jes Staley Former Barclays CEO Jes Staley lost his appeal against a ban from senior roles in financial services for allegedly misleading the regulator over his relationship with Epstein. ( ) JPMorgan and Barclays chief executive Jes Staley resigned as Barclays chief executive in 2021 following an investigation by regulators into his links with Epstein. The American banker was later banned from the UK financial sector following a failed legal appeal last year. He has also been sued by JPMorgan — the largest bank in the United States — which claimed he concealed information about Epstein's misconduct. Mr Staley attended Epstein-hosted gatherings and exchanged around 1,200 emails with the disgraced financier over four years, some of which talked about Disney characters and photos of young women, according to court documents. He has denied knowing about Epstein's criminal activities. Resigned: Joichi Ito Joichi Ito accepted donations from Epstein in 2019. ( ) Media Lab director and professor at MIT Joichi Ito, a Japanese entrepreneur, resigned as the director of the Media Lab and a professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in March after the university accepted donations from Epstein in 2019. In a post on his website, the venture capitalist said the donations had been accepted with the approval of senior administrators and that he had not violated any laws or policies. Selling business: Casey Wasserman Casey Wasserman is selling his sports marketing and talent agency following the release of flirtatious emails between him and Maxwell. ( ) Chairperson of the Wasserman Media Group Casey Wasserman, the top US official overseeing the 2028 Olympic Games in Los Angeles, faces calls to step down after the release of flirtatious emails between him and Ghislaine Maxwell as early as 2003. The Hollywood mogul and his then-wife flew on a humanitarian mission to Africa aboard Epstein's plane at the invitation of the Clinton Foundation, a review by the 2028 LA Olympics Organising Committee found. In February, Mr Wasserman announced he was selling his sports marketing and talent agency after clients including Chappell Roan said the company would no longer represent them. The company, formally known as Wasserman, was rebranded to The Team in March. Resigned: Bernard Kruger Dr Bernard Kruger stepped down from multiple roles following the Epstein fallout. ( ) Doctor at Atria Health and Research Institute, and board member of Sollis Health Bernard Kruger resigned from two roles at two medical practices in March after files revealed he gave Epstein VIP treatment, often allowing him to book appointments without using names.

Academia

Resigned: Larry Summers Former US Treasury secretary Larry Summers. ( ) Professor at Harvard University Larry Summers resigned from his post at Harvard University in February following scrutiny over his ties to Epstein. He flew on Epstein's jet several times as far back as 1998 and met with him to discuss economic and business matters while he served as president of Harvard. No evidence of wrongdoing by him has surfaced. In November, the economist — who served as US treasury secretary under former president Bill Clinton — also resigned from the board of OpenAI, the developer of the ChatGPT artificial intelligence tool, after Harvard announced its review. Resigned: Richard Axel Dr Richard Axel is stepping down as an investigator at the Howard Hughes Medical Institute. ( ) Co-director of Columbia University's neuroscience institute Richard Axel resigned as co-director of Columbia University's Zuckerman Mind Brain Behavior Institute in February, describing his past association with Epstein as a "serious error in judgement". "What has emerged about Epstein's appalling conduct, the harm that he has caused to so many people, makes my association with him all the more painful and inexcusable," he said in a statement. The university said it "has seen no evidence that Dr Axel violated any university policy or the law". The Nobel laureate also announced that he would be stepping down as an investigator at the Howard Hughes Medical Institute. Resigned: David A Ross Chair of the MFA Art Practice program at New York's School of Visual Arts An anonymous business person profile. ( ) David A Ross resigned as chair of the MFA Art Practice program at New York's School of Visual Arts after documents released in February revealed his ties with Epstein. The art museum curator and director met Epstein in the mid 1990s when he was the director of the Whitney Museum of American Art in New York, Mr Ross wrote in a statement. In emails from 2009, Epstein suggests an exhibition called "Statutory" that would feature "girls and boys ages 14-25, where they look nothing like their true ages". Ross replied, "You are incredible", and noted that actor Brooke Shields posed nude at age 10.

Law

Resigned: Kathryn Ruemmler Kathryn Ruemmler was a former White House counsel to Democratic President Barack Obama. ( ) Chief legal officer at Goldman Sachs Kathryn Ruemmler resigned as the top lawyer at Goldman Sachs after revelations she accepted gifts from Epstein and gave him public relations advice across five years. The former White House counsel to Barack Obama says she dealt with Epstein as a defence attorney and was not aware of any ongoing criminal conduct. Resigned: Brad Karp Emails show Brad Karp attended dinners with Epstein. ( ) Chairperson of Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison The head of powerful Wall Street law firm Paul, Weiss resigned after emails revealed longstanding personal and business communications with Epstein through 2019. The lawyer attended dinners with Epstein and sought his help getting a job on a Woody Allen film, the emails show. The firm said Mr Karp regretted his interactions with Epstein and never witnessed nor participated in any misconduct.

Giufrre is among the 1,200 survivors and their family members who appear in the Epstein files — a cache of about 3.5 million pages made public so far. The US Justice Department continues to withhold millions more.

Since her death, Giuffre's family says they hope the world remembers her as "a fierce warrior in the fight against sexual abuse and sex trafficking".
